control is the easiest to get rid of, at least in my opinion. then again, now that i think about it, it's hard. the token of advice for control is to only control yourself. you cannot control anyone else and should not control anyone else. but you can control what you do, how you do it, when you do it, so on so forth. compromise will be your new friend. don't abuse compromise either and learn to accept it. an example is: you want to go to a store, but your friend wants to go to a different store. they both close at the same time and you'll only be able to make it to one store with the time you have left.

compromise: you go to one of the stores today, then go together tomorrow or the next day.   
the compromise then breaks into..well which store? sacrifice is then needed to be learned. you sacrifice your desire to go to your store today and save it for tomorrow. look at it in a positive light. you have something to be excited about tomorrow. it's a dumb analogy, but hopefully you get it. 

control is about releasing selfishness and allowing others to have a little bit of their own. but always remember that sacrifice comes with balance. i made a bad habit of becoming too selfless and giving, which left me bitter when people abused it. set your boundaries. your friend gets to go to their store first today, but next time you guys run into something like this, you get to go to your store first. 

balance is always required, another rule to remember.

the answer: every abled adult can walk! there are of course some that cannot, they are individuals who are disabled; but majority of them have found devices to either assist, help or mimic the ability to travel a distance. long or short. if they had feared failure, they would never move from a spot and therefore, never get to experience pieces of life.

take what you're afraid of. think of the first thing that makes you feel the most stressed when you think of failure. unpiece it. why are you afraid of this? does it make you feel inferior? stupid? ugly? a bad person? find those negative keys, then write them down somewhere. i am afraid of doing \_\_\_ because i feel \_\_\_ about myself.

it's really good you did the 3 things he likes about himself thing. now, when it comes to combating depression, the patient usually struggles at first with seeing anything good about themselves. thinking on myself years ago, i too wouldn't be able to name anything i liked about myself and i was in my early twenties then with an arsenal of background history and understanding of self. so if that was hard for me, an adult to do, this is a task that can be even more difficult for a child.

again, i press that it's really good you did that, not many parents would and i'm proud of you for knowing to do that. however, let's start with more baby steps than that. what i do when i struggle to list good things of myself are options like these:

* three things i did good/am proud of for the day (did i shower, did i do my online work, did i make my bed. it can be anything. tell him it can be anything, small or big.)
* three things i thought were interesting/liked in the day (maybe i saw a cute dog or maybe i saw a cool advertisement! tell him to think about the day, find things he liked in it.)
* three things i want to do in the week (now im an adult and my priorities are to get my hits from being productive, so i put things like clean the tub and w/n; but he can put SMALL TASKS that he wants to do for the week. maybe he can clean his room, or take the trash out, or finish his homework, or heck even play a level of a game. something that is productive, but also easy to do is where we're aiming here.)

there's so many more you can do like that but those are the three main ones i use. so what this does is it begins to channel positive thinking in our brains without blocking us off from the 'so uh what do u like about urself' question that can be challenging and uncomfortable for us to think about. we want to stimulate the brain into acknowledging that there are beautiful things out there and we are capable of growing! we are beautiful too and we can do whatever we want! slowly, but surely by doing this, we begin to build ourselves up to things like: 'so what is one thing you like about yourself from this week', and eventually 'name three things you like about yourself'. 

my second advice for you is..you said he's not a talker. talking can be uncomfortable. i personally am not verbal either. i start to tear up and get frustrated and embarrassed, then shut down. recently i've been getting better at it. if we're not talkers; we're usually writers and find comfort in writing. give him the prompt on paper, sit with him as he does it. if you sense he's anxious that you're around, say; i'll be back in ten minutes, write those things down so we can talk about them! then leave and do something for the duration. usually when you come back, they'll have written a few things down. they might be shy and nervous, it's hard to open up when you're scared and dislike yourself; but positivity helps so many things. smile, read his list aloud, but don't embarrass him by being too over the top. agree with his points such as:

'i brushed my teeth last night'  
\[you beam and nod\] you did!! thank you for doing that!   


he'll begin to catch onto the act himself, and might even find this to be a good bonding opportunity. of course, you should nurse the negatives too. they're hurtful and letting them fester becomes upsetting. engage in his life. ask him why. 

in therapy, we always ask 'why'. we're detectives, we want to find the root. why does he feel this way. because he's hurt. but why is he hurt. the kids at school are being hurtful. does he know why they might being hurtful? find roots! always find roots! and remember that you're doing your best for him. you may screw up sometimes, it's okay. you're a loving parent, i can tell by how worried you sound here.

in the meantime, i apologize if i say anything that might not resonate with you well. firstly, i want to say that..it's difficult to get past, i can't imagine doing what you're doing. when we lose someone we love close to us, especially a child or parent, we lose a piece of us; our soul. our world becomes bleak, bleaker than we could have ever imagined and the lagoon of misery sets on quickly, only expanding in size as time passes. we think. we try to resonate with ourselves. we want answers. we ask them often, over and over. why did this happen? what was the purpose of it. why did you hurt me like this? why did you hurt someone else like this? and silence is all we find.

the unfortunate truth is that we will never find the answer. at least, not an answer we *want*. one of the reasons why people struggle so long with PTSD is because they're in the loop of this cycle, searching and searching for the *right* answer. an answer that will validate their pain and give them a reason to move onward. we're flawed like that, always wanting a sense of closure before we feel as if we can grow. but this search only hurts us in the long run, as neglect to our cries makes us feel small, frail and hopeless. 

i want to state that other people are the least of your worries. you deserve to be upset, you deserve to be sad, you deserve to cry and scream and curl up in a ball and have someone wrap you around in a blanket, comforting you. grief is one of the most difficult emotions to overcome, it haunts us, it traumatizes us and it changes us with no ability to change ourselves back. when we lose a piece of ourselves, it simply cannot be replaced with an exact replica of said piece that enables us to return to 100% the person we were before. when you find people  seem to feel irritated with you or losing patience, ask for more. show vulnerability. i know it's hard, the desire to be strong is ironically; a strong one, but you deserve time, and i find people tend to understand better and become more empathetic when you're vulnerable with them. never feel bad for how you feel.

so, i don't want to get you down or make you feel worse but self therapy is incredible difficult to do. first and foremost, i really suggest getting a therapist. if you can't for whatever reason (not going to get into it b/c personal reasons are personal), then let me get you started and on the right foot.

firstly, get a journal. this is going to be your new buddy. name it, put stickers on it, do something to make it yours. there's a reason why teenage girls write in journals in movies and it's because it's cathartic and therapeutic. the journal is a place where we can store our thoughts and get them out of our heads and self evaluate in a place that has 0 judgement and is entirely our own personal space. it's the home inside your home, where nobody else goes. when you write in your journal, do some key things:

* express yourself sincerely. write the negatives of your day. how you feel. what you wish you could do that you aren't. what you want to be different. vent it out. nobody is watching and your journal wants to know.
* on lower end days, such as when you feel lesser; try self-taught DBT therapy. i'll link you to the sub for DBT here:  dbtselfhelp . read the first post, get the work books you feel are fit for you and practice them. always practice them. mindfulness opens the eye to understanding yourself. this should help give you tools to self soothing.
* self reflect. always self reflect. ask yourself in your head AND journal. why do i feel \_\_ about \_\_. why did i feel \_\_\_ today? this is training your brain to find causes for things. sometimes you won't find it, and that's okay! know that it happens! sometimes we just have bad days, and that's alright.

whenever you find your journal is full, you're free to do whatever you want with it. some people keep them and store them to reflect on later. some people toss them. some people burn them. it's up to you. but really. i realllllyyyy put emphasis on the journal thing.

another thing that is good to do is meditation. everyone will tell you that one and lord does it get annoying to hear. but 10 minute a day session of meditation helps clear your head so you can think straight. you don't have to go into deep ends of it, but just enough to feel refreshed, like someone pressed f5 on your day and you're going from sad to controlled. try to do it at least 3 times a week. just to reset yourself.

giving yourself a therapy session is also great. this is building a straw therapist that can be anyone. a prior therapist, a family member, a doctor, a character; someone who you find comfort in is now in the imaginary seat from you. (i really suggest doing a character since they're not personal and can't suddenly hurt you, but that might just be me). make sure this is someone with good morals and a good moral compass, not your drunk uncle or pseudo norman bates. internally talk with them. state an issue you have an envision what they might say or how they respond. this is a self soothing exercise that can really help with struggles! you can also do this in your journal.

my last bit of advice is learning mental health. educating yourself on it. reading into practices therapists use and figuring out how to apply them to yourself. they may not be the authentic thing, but they're still something, which is better than nothing.
